curriculum.lesson_evidence: Rhythm and rhyme schemes are patterns of stress and sound. Year 8 students can mark a simple scheme (AABB, ABAB) and explain whether rhyme tightens pace, creates humour or feels forced.
curriculum.scope_limit: Proposed Stage 4 NESA English alignment using catalogue outcome codes (EN4-*); content-point mapping and independent NESA verification remain pending.

lesson.child_mission: Rhythm and rhyme schemes are patterns of stress and sound. Year 8 students can mark a simple scheme (AABB, ABAB) and explain whether rhyme tightens pace, creates humour or feels forced.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same strategy to an unfamiliar topic or audience, then compare the effect of two different choices.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Mark the rhyme scheme of an 8-line extract and judge one rhyme as effective or forced with a reason.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: scheme labelled correctly; judgement tied to meaning, not only “it rhymes.”

CHECK
Assuming all good poems must rhyme, or praising rhyme that damages sense.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Independently rewrite four lines two ways (rhymed vs free) and argue which better serves your narrative poem’s mood.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Rhythm and rhyme schemes are patterns of stress and sound. Year 8 students can mark a simple scheme (AABB, ABAB) and explain whether rhyme tightens pace, creates humour or feels forced.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Independently rewrite four lines two ways (rhymed vs free) and argue which better serves your narrative poem’s mood. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using rhythm on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample error: Assuming all good poems must rhyme, or praising rhyme that damages sense.. Correction: Strong answer: scheme labelled correctly;. Why it helps the audience is stated.

Parent: Likely misconception: Assuming all good poems must rhyme, or praising rhyme that damages sense. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating rhythm on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with rhythm, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about rhythm with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for rhythm. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.explain:
Rhythm and rhyme schemes are patterns of stress and sound. Year 8 students can mark a simple scheme (AABB, ABAB) and explain whether rhyme tightens pace, creates humour or feels forced.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
